titleStmt.title: Interview with Benjamin Colkitt, II, April 5 (year not available)
titleStmt.author: C. Kay Uhles

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Benjamin Colkitt, II was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.head: Interview with Benjamin Colkitt, II [April 5 (year not available)]

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Let me tell you why I would do this on my death bed, and I may be. We just looked at a letter from a friend of mine that he wrote on his death bed. And I don't know what his connection was with the Smithsonian, but here a few years ago, when they were restoring the Enola Gay to display it, one of the curators in there wanted to display the Enola Gay to be an apology to the Japanese people for using the A-bomb on them, which to me just shows a complete lack of knowledge of history. So I think there is a crying need to get history out to the kids. Now, one of the best programs I've run into is, in a couple of cases, I've had a high school student that came to interview me, and his class assignment was for the student to interview a World War II veteran to get, you know, one-on-one information on World War II. It's a wonderful program. It was part of the mandatory school work.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yes. And it's a good thing they're doing that. Let me introduce everybody in the room and --

sp.speaker: Vicki Hartmetz
sp.p: Let me try the tripod one more time. (Pause.)

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What I'm going to do, Ben, is I'm going to introduce everybody in the room and introduce you, and just set the scene, first of all, the dates and where we are. I'm not going to give your address or anything on the record -- (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: -- and then we're going to ask you some specific questions and get specific events that you might remember from your experiences. And I'll just go through these questions. The hope is to limit it to ninety minutes. Today is Thursday, April the 5th, at 10 a.m., and we are in Aurora. Is that correct, Ben?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Aurora, Colorado, and we are interviewing Mr. Ben Colkitt, Junior, right?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Correct.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Junior. And then would you spell your name for us?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: C-o-l-k-i-t-t.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. Thank you. And so, Mr. Colkitt, we're going to introduce the court reporter, who is Joyce Martin, and our videographer is Vicki Hartmetz. And so we're just going to ask you some questions about your -- and my name is Kay Uhles, and I'm the director of education at Denver Academy of Court Reporting in Denver, Colorado.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: First of all, were you enlisted? Did you enlist or were you drafted into the military?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. I went directly into the Naval Aviation Cadet Program. Now, this was in early 1942, a couple weeks after Pearl Harbor, and we were enlisted as Seamen Second V-5. Now, V-5 is an indication of aviation cadet. And we wore a uniform with no insignia on it.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: There was no insignia on it?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. This was -- they were just getting into high gear, getting into the war, and everything was just getting organized. So I was in the second group to be called up, so we were helping to build a place as we ran through it. And the program was that we started through preflight school. And the one I went to was at the University of Georgia, and that was more or less an indoctrination, a boot indoctrination, into the naval service and to say we were Seamen Second V-5, but we had no rank. We were just a new species that they created. The preflight was an introduction to the Navy, really, and physical conditionings. And from there, we went to primary flight training. And I went to Naval Air Station Anacostia.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Where was that again, Ben?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Naval Air Station Anacostia. That's in D.C., Washington D.C.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: We were housed on the base, but we were trucked in school buses to outlying fields. They were dirt strip airports, just getting organized, just starting the program, and the preflights where we -- we were introduced to flying, and we were soloed. And we completed that school and then went to basic training at Pensacola Naval Air Station and stayed through getting my wings at Pensacola. And at that time -- up to that time, the program had taken several years. Well, my group was pushed through in a couple weeks less than a year. They were in a hurry for people the age of yesterday.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: How did that feel? Did you feel like you were prepared with being pushed through like that?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Hey, I was 21.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Let's go get them, huh?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Thought I'd died and gone to heaven.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: So we went through aviation training at Pensacola, got wings, and the situation was such that my entire class immediately became instructors. We were a student one day, and then the next day, we were instructors. They were that short of people. And this is during the time of the Battle of Midway and several of the other battles, and they needed people. Needed them in a hurry.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And now what date are we talking about now? Is this --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I got -- went into the Navy in 1942, got my wings in May of '43, and then I went to work.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. Where?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I didn't care for an instructor and I wanted to get in the war, so I got into -- went through fighter recon school at Pensacola. And from there, was sent out to the fleet on the West Coast.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And what ship did you wind up on?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: When? I've been on a bunch of ships.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: The first one. How about the first one? What was that experience like?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: The first one was a little weird, because needless to say, in '43, '44, all of our main carriers were busy. So the Navy got two side-wheeler excursion boats on Lake Michigan, put a flight deck and arresting gear on it, and that was our initial carrier training. This was the Sable and the Wolverine. And that's why there are so many naval airplanes in the bottom of Lake Michigan, because this was an initial carrier qualification. They put a bunch of them in the bottom of the lake there. But it was -- they put arresting gear on the top, no catapults, and made a deck run to get off.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And the arresting gear, is that what stops you?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: The hook snags to stop the airplane. So that was our initial carrier qualification. And then out to the West Coast for assignment to coast squadron, and eventually wound up in Fighter Squadron No. 1, VF 1, on board the Bennington CV 20. And the Bennington was in Task Force 38. That was Admiral McCain's task group. Task Group 38 would be, take the destination of 38 when one admiral had it; when his relief admiral took over, it became 58. So the same group of ships is referred to as either Task Force 38 or 58, depending on who was in command. But anyhow, the task force consisted of four or five task groups, and each task group had five or six carriers. And by the time I got out there, the task force was operating off the east coast of Japan. As we found out later, we were getting ready for the invasion, which we found out later was scheduled for somewhere around October or November.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: So how many months did you have to prepare for the invasion?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, the surrender was in August, and they found out later, the invasion was scheduled for somewhere around October. So as we found out, what we were doing was working over in Japan, taking out as much of their operation as we could before we went ashore.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: So did you -- so you flew missions over Japan?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Was that -- did you see combat? Was there combat or fight against you?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, they shot at me and I shot at them, so I guess you could call it combat.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: I guess you could. I would.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Any close calls or any specific events that you remember in any of those missions?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, when you're that young, you don't know what a close call is.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: So getting shot at isn't too safe, but other than that -- but it's really a roll of the dice.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What type of airplane did you fly?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I was flying a Hellcat at that time.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: A Hellcat?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. And I'm assuming that's a helicopter?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: No. I'm assuming wrong?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: That's the fighter.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Which is the yellow --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Right here.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Oh, I see, the picture. Oh, there's a picture. Okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: The Hellcat shot down more Japanese airplanes than any of the other airplanes out there.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you shoot down a Japanese airplane?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. I couldn't get there fast enough. A couple times we ventured out, and the Japs -- you could see the balls of fire falling down, and I knew it was too late, which is kind of interesting, really, because one of the biggest attacks we had was a week or so after the surrender. You know, after the surrender, a bunch of the Japanese pilots had no intention of surrendering, so they mounted some of the biggest attacks on the fleet that we saw. And that's where we saw some action.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you -- so when you were 21, you didn't feel any of the stress? Were you nervous? Were you ever fearful? Or 21, you're pretty --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, yeah. You've got to be fearful. If you're fearless, you have no caution, and if you have no caution, you're dangerous. So you need to be alert. You need to realize that things can get a little dicey, so it's a necessity. But it's a necessity. But I haven't found anybody to tell you they wasn't scared.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: How about your -- any members of your unit or any instructors that stand out in your mind, any authority figures that --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, a squadron skipper. He was -- he was different. He had been an enlisted pilot during the '30s. And at that time, the Navy had enlisted pilots, as well as commissioned officer pilots. And so when the war started, he was commissioned. So he was -- having been in the Navy that long, he was about, I'd say, in his late 30s. So to we kids, he was an old man. And we found out later, the military recovered a Zero that had force landed in the Aleutians, and he brought it back to California and got it back into flying condition. And my ex-skipper had been one of the test pilots flying this, getting an idea of the capabilities of the Zero so we could work up defensive tactics against it. So that was impressive.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What about when you were on the carrier, what was a day like for you? Did you -- were you sitting around waiting for assignments and going out on missions? Did you know in advance what you were doing during the day?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: We knew in advance by about a day or two. We did not know about future operations, because if we were -- they didn't want us to have that information in case we were captured. So we were normally kept in the dark about future operations. But you could -- you could figure a lot out.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Were you ever captured?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Or never had any close calls with the Japanese or anything, or Germans?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Other than getting shot at, no.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. What did you do before the war? You were 19 when you went in, so not a lot of experience there, but . . .

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I was a senior at Davidson College when Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: At Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: When Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. And where was your college?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Davidson College near Charlotte, North Carolina. So as soon as I could, I got through the Navy, and said, "I'm ready, take me." And they asked me where I was in college, and I said, "Well, in my final semester." And they were a lot smarter than I was, and they said, "Well, you go back, graduate, and send us a letter when you graduate, and we'll send you orders, and you can start to work in the Navy." So I did. And a week after I graduated from Davidson, I had my orders -- this was in May of that year -- and friends in Navy and stayed there for over 22 years.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Were your parents happy that you were going into the military?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What happened?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Fortunately, right after Pearl Harbor, the next month, I turned 21, so . . .

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Couldn't keep you home, could they?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, the thing is this: My only ambition up to that point had been to be a military aviator. So as far as I'm concerned, the war is just a convenience, 'cause that's where I was headed regardless. So it worked out great for me.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family when you --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: You know, that's something -- that's something the kids ought to learn about. When we were out at sea, we were supplied by auxiliary ships, which would highline the stuff over -- the supplies over to us, including the mail. So the only mail contact we had was when the ships would bring the mail out, highline it over the ships. So sometimes it would be 30 days or so before we would get a letter. Nowadays, on a ship anywhere in the world, go up to the wall, pick up a cell phone, call home. So it was -- the war was really hard on the girls because they had no idea what was happening to their guys. Nowadays, you got instant contact.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you know your present wife Donna at that time?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. No, we met during Korea.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Now, I understand, she was -- was she in the military or was she a civilian service?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: She was an ensign.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: An ensign in the military, in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. When she got in, the Navy knew that they were going to have to take women into the service, so they started this program, conditioning some of these girls as line officers. So she was in the second class to report for duty. So she was a history maker herself.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And we're going to get her story, too.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: We're going to get that as soon as we can, too.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yeah. What was the food like on the carriers?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Was it? Was it freeze-dried? That was before the freeze-dried. Did you have real eggs, or were they --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: You got to be kidding. We had freeze-dried eggs. We had reconstituted milk, which is a real experience. Course, you've heard the stories about Spam. That was true. Spam was a staple in those days.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: There's probably still a few cans from around that era still around here.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. We were resupplied at sea. Stores were highlined over, so most the stuff was dried, not too much fresh.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: How did you ever survive on it?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Didn't know any better.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you ever get used to it, or was it just --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. Took it for granted. That's the way it was.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And did you have plenty of food and plenty of supplies?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And they took care of you in that way?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, that's something else kids don't realize. You have a fighting force out there, the tip of the spear, if you will, only because they have the supply support. 'Cause I think during World War II, something like one guy in ten was actually in combat. The rest were in the support. And if you don't have support, you don't have a fighting force. So an awful lot of jobs in the military, unless you're doing combat, are essential. The same is true today.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Do you think the numbers are still about the same, one in ten?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I would say so. I'm sure you have a number of people to keep one man in the fight. You gotta have them.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And how long a period of time did you stay on the carrier -- were you there for six months, a year -- without coming home?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: It depended on what was going on. Nowadays, the common tour is about six months, and their groups are rotated off the carrier every six months. And that's really for maintenance and to refresh the pilots. And during the war on the Bennington, there was a new air carrier -- air group on there every six months. And the ship's company had been on there since the ship had been built. So normally, the ship's company would be on there for several years. As a pilot in the air group, you could usually figure on maybe six months.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And what did you do for entertainment while you were on the ship?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, read, I guess.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Read?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. This is before the days of DVDs and all that good stuff. We didn't have any.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: They didn't have any reel-to-reel movies or anything?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: We had movies, yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: They didn't bring any entertainment on? Bob Hope didn't come on the ship or anything?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. The USO shows went through the Pacific, and those were wonderful. But the standard uniform to go to a USO show is some helmet and poncho, because out in the South Pacific, you'd have a shower just about every night, and nobody was going to leave.So you just took a poncho and sat there in the rainstorm and watched.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Any particular USO show that sticks out in your mind?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Bob Hope, of course.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Bob Hope, yeah. Yeah. I guess he brought his bevy of beauties along with him. Benjamin Colkitt, II:: Yeah, I think there were some girls there.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Was there -- when you were flying these missions, was there anything that you took along for good luck, or any ritual or anything for good luck that you did?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. It was a job, like jumping in your truck and going to work.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you go do anything special during your leave time? Did you -- where did you have your leave when you got off the ship?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, of course, during the war, we didn't get leave, so we stayed out where we were. But leave was just like anyone's vacation, no different than it would be now.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. And you said you were in the Navy for 44 years?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Oh, I'm sorry. I misunderstood.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I just look that old. 22 years.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: I'm sorry, 22 years. I misspoke.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yes, okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Really the reason I retired was 'cause they told me I was too old to fly.They want young fighter pilots. They don't want old guys. So I had gotten to the point where Iwas too senior and too old for front-line squadron, so I retired. Nowadays, they can stay a little bit longer. But it was a real youth program then.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: In one of the e-mails you sent me, you said that later you were a Panther pilot. Benjamin Colkitt, II:: Yes. That's the squadron up at the top here, F9F. It was one of the first transition jets, when the carriers transitioned from prop aircraft to jets on the carrier. C. Kay Uhles:: And that was over Korea, you said?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Any particular experience that sticks out in your mind during that time?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yes. The one that sticks in my mind probably sticks in all the career military people minds now. During Korea and actions after that, the wars were being run by politicians. And we were flying strikes out of Korea. We knew we couldn't win the war. The politicians wouldn't let us. And doing the same thing as Vietnam, we got the same thing in Iraq. So that sticks in my mind, as well as military people.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And how does that affect military people when you're in the service and you're recognizing that?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, I think the American public is very lucky, 'cause the guys are very serious about their career. And the attitude I developed during Korea was, I know we can't win, and there's nothing I can do about it. I'm working for the Navy, they give me my orders, I carry them out. I didn't give it any thought. And the guys are having to do that now.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And did you do any service in Vietnam during the Vietnam conflict?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No, I retired.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Before that?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: During Vietnam, yeah. I had gotten too old. The Navy told me I was too old to fly, so I retired, and flew for United for 28 years.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Wow. A lot of service in the air, huh?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Fifty-five years.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: How about in the Mediterranean during the Cold War? One of your e-mails mentions that.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Any particular experience you remember during that time?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, that was very interesting.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: In what way?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, we were -- we were flying with loaded guns and we knew somebody could send the balloon up any time.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Send the balloon up. What --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Start the war going on.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And so that was the jargon, being a balloon, sending a balloon up?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. Saying was, we were here waiting for the balloon to go up. That means that would be when the combat would start.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And from whom? What country would send the balloon up?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, we didn't know. But I was in the Mediterranean fleet, Sixth Fleet. We were cruising around the Mediterranean. Really, it's a show of force. And I remember the day before the elections in Italy, the ships lined up, and we went steaming up the coast, just off the coast, where everybody on the beach could see us. We weren't trying to influence the election or anything, but we were just showing off the fleet. And they did stay democratic.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And what year was this?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Late '40s?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I guess somewhere around '48 -- '47, '48, somewhere along in there.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. And any particularly humorous events happen during your service? By the way, did you ever put an airplane in Lake Michigan?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Nope.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Not one of yours down there?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Nope. You know, I flew for 55 years, and I flew in combat in two wars, flew night fighters off a carrier, and the most dangerous time I ever had was driving on the freeway.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. Came closer to getting in trouble on the freeway than I did in flying.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: So landing on the carriers did not feel as dangerous?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, there are two grades: pass and fail. So . . .

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: It's pretty obvious which grade you get, I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What was it like --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: That was the thing that really blew Donna's mind the first time I took her down to Pensacola, because the air station graveyard is right by the main gate. So the first thing you see when you go in the air station there in Pensacola is the graveyard. Like I told her, those are the guys that flunked. And she never quite got over that, but it was true.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: But during the -- particularly, during the World War II, we took an awful lot of losses, operationally, because the business just -- it's a hazardous business, so we lost an awful lot of people just operational.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: In what way? Can you tell us about it?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Crashes, yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: So the crashes?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And so the planes would -- would the planes just go off the carrier or are you talking --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Oh, you got all kinds of ways.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: -- midair?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: There's all kinds of ways to crash an airplane, yeah. I know one of my pilots got target fixation. One of the things that can happen is diving on a target and, you know, just another second to get on. Just another second to be on it. And the guys wait too late and they fly into the target. So I lost one friend that way. Well, actually, a couple.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What was it like the first time, your very first time, of landing on a carrier, not in your training, but on the big carriers and that hook catching the wire?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Is it?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: The Navy has a saying about it, but I -- we better leave that off the record.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: They might be interested in it, too.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. I'll get busted.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: We won't push the issue.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Needless to say, it's the biggest thrill.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. And what about taking off, is that just as exhilarating, taking off on a big ship?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you ever miss -- did the hook ever miss and you'd have to take off again?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: That's part of the program, yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Wow. Amazing. Do you have --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Incidentally, if you want to see a tailhook, I have one in the garage. C. Kay Uhles:: I'd love to. I don't know -- is it huge?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: I mean, is it -- so we couldn't carry it around or anything?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. But I carry it in my Bug in the sunroof. I was at the naval air station in North Island when I retired. And in the officer's club there, they have a tailhook mounted on a plaque mounted over the bar, which I thought was real neat. So when I retired in North Island, there was a junkyard there. So I went down, and the guy behind the desk, I said, "I'm retiring, I'd like to get a tailhook." And he looked at me with a real funny look, and he said,"Just a minute, Commander." He went in the back, and I could hear him dialing on the phone. Pretty soon, he came back in with a funny look on his face and said, "What kind do you want?" "Iwant one off of a Panther," because that was the last operational plane I flew. So pretty soon,he came out with it, and I opened up my sunroof and stuck it in my Bug. Got a lot of looks as Iwas driving down the freeway. Brought it home, walked in. She said, "What are you going to do with that?" And I said, "I'm going to mount it over the fireplace, of course." It's still in the garage.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: You didn't mount it on top of the car either?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And you said you retired a commander. Was that the rank?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. Did you become particularly close to any one person that you've kept in contact with over the years?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: My wife.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Your wife. That's a good one. What about the organizations you belong to?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: You form -- you form close friendships in the military. And you may go years and then run into an old friend. So friendships in the military really last a lot longer than they do in a civilian world. So usually, whenever you go to a new duty station, at least a couple people are around that usually you knew them before. Just a real nice situation.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: So what year did you meet your wife Donna?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: 1950. Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And did you serve on the same ship?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Nope. After World War II, a lot of -- most of the people that were in the military during World War II were Reserves. So after the war was over, Reserves went home, and some of us were getting an opportunity to turn regular. And those of us that became regulars, then, were sent to a line school. It was a school the Navy put together to give military naval education comparable to the academy. Now, most of us were college graduates, so line school essentially gave us the military part of academy training. And at the same time, the Navy had their backs to the wall, and they knew they were going to have to take females into the service, and that's when they started the women's line officer school. And bless their souls, they put it at the same place as the line school. Now, I still think -- I still think we had a friend in BUPERS that organized the schools that way, because about over 90 percent of the girls in those first classes that came through wound up married within a year.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Really. And did you say you had a friend -- a friend that set it up so the girls came to the same place?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: That's what we suspected.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: That's what you suspected? And did you mention a name?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Oh, okay. I misunderstood.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: But bless their hearts wherever they are.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Hallelujah. It worked out well for you and --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, in the class that Donna was in, the classes were, I think, 24 people. And they were selected out of a group of well over 500 applicants.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Very selective?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: They got the cream of the crop.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yeah. And so how did you meet her? Did you just go up to her one day or --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, as I tell my grandkids, I picked her up in the bar in the officer's club.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: That sounds like a good place back then.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And did you start going out?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, it was kind of --

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you know immediately?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: It was kind of funny, but we had been out in the war, out at sea duty, all kinds of raunchy places, and here we are in line school in Newport, Rhode Island. Thought we'd died and gone to heaven. And then they bring this girl school in there. Well, there really is a heaven. That's when we met.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you know right away it was the one?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I think we were engaged a couple weeks.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: And that just blows the mind for the grandkids.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Are you okay? Do you want to take a break?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No, I'm fine.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. And within a couple weeks, you were engaged?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yep. And married.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And married?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. How long does it take to make up your mind?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: You almost beat an uncle of mine. Yeah. They did the same thing. So where were you married?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Newport.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Right there?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: In the naval chapel. We went back there, to Newport, and the bar at the O Club is still there, doing business, and the church -- the naval chapel burned down. So I guess there's a story there. We had a big naval wedding with swords, whites, all that.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And you have how many children?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Four.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And where are they now?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, my son, Benjamin, is an attorney here in town. No. 1 daughter is a doctor on Bainbridge Island in Washington. No. 2 daughter is a school teacher in -- near Kingstown, New York. And No. 3 daughter is an RN in the hospital at Albany. Not a pilot in the bunch.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Not a pilot in the bunch?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Couldn't care less.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Interesting how it skips sometimes, isn't it? Do you have -- I think you or your wife mentioned to me that you do have some photographs. Do you have them right here or not? It doesn't look like it.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Man, do I have photographs. I've got all kinds of photographs.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. Any -- any one stand out in your mind that you want to tell us about?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Talking about photographs?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. I had to burn those when I got married. Well, the pictures I took of the prisoner-of-war camps were -- I thought were kind of neat. Did you see those? Right after the surrender, we knew that the prisoner-of-war camps were on the main island of Japan, but we didn't know exactly where they were. So flying a photographic recon fighter, I was sent out to -- well, first of all, to locate the camps and take a picture of them, so we could pinpoint them to go out and get the guys. And I've got some pictures that I can show you of some of the camps we took. We should have all been killed, 'cause we -- we decided we'd throw the guys some newspapers and notes, people sending out all that stuff. So we were flying the fighter with one hand with flaps down and canopy open a hundred feet above the ground, leaning out, and threw these packages down. And it's a wonder we didn't kill ourselves and the guys on the ground. C. Kay Uhles:: And was somebody -- go ahead.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: A year after that, I got a card from one of the guys.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: One of the prisoners of war?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah, that picked up one of the packets.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: How did he find you, do you know?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. I had my address on the card --

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: -- that I dropped.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you stay in touch with him?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And when you were dropping these cards and these packets out of the airplane, somebody was taking pictures --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: -- of the camps?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Guys in the planes.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yeah. So that sounds like a letter of gratitude --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: -- you got for helping them out. Anything else like that that you got? Did you win any awards or medals or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. That's what we were supposed to do.

sp.speaker: Candace James
sp.p: Dad, what are these awards up here? What are those awards for?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Just stuff.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Do you want to tell us what those are in the frames? The medals in the frames? Benjamin Colkitt, II::Let's take a break.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Let's take a break? Okay. (Telephone rings.)

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: So this is the prisoner camp here?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Could I look at the rest of these, Ben?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yes, of course. (A break was taken.)

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: When I started, I went out to Guam. Before we went on the Bennington, the ship we were riding on came into the harbor there at Guam, and there was a Hornet with the first 30 or 50 feet of the flight deck bent over the bow that had gotten caught in the typhoon, and there was a heavy cruiser there that was about gone, and the Hornet's flight deck was bent over the bow. So they sent a ship back to the States for repairs, and they put some of us on board the Hornet to fly the airplanes off. So we flew them back into Guam.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No, huh-uh.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Who was the astronaut, Shepard? Which astronaut was it that you guys lived across the field from?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Oh, John Glenn. We were neighbors down in Corpus.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: John Glenn?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. We partied with them.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: You got some stories about John Glenn? We're not on the record right now, so . . .

sp.speaker: Joyce Martin
sp.p: Yes, we are.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I was in a training squadron with John before he became an astronaut.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: So what year would that be?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: 1950, '51. That's when John had hair.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: He really did truly have hair at one time. So did you keep in touch with him at all when he was circling the world or anything?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No, never did. But I didn't answer the question on the medals. Three air medals.

sp.speaker: Candace James
sp.p: All right, Dad. Why don't you tell us about these medals that you have.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: What did I do with the citation?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: I've got one in my hand right here. Is this what you're looking for?

sp.speaker: Candace James
sp.p: Oh, look at this. Mom put it on the back here. All right. So there's three air medals, Asiatic Pacific Campaign Medal. That's the star.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, the air medals were the only combat awards. The other campaigner ribbons was "just he was there" medals.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Candace James
sp.p: And so it says, beyond that, it's World War II Victory Medal, a Navy Occupation Service Medal, China Service Medal -- I didn't know you had that.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: You never asked me.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: They're just campaign medals.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: National Defense Service Medal, Korean Service Medal, and a Korean Unit Citation. All right. And it says the dates of service were 2-28-42 to 6-30-64. All right. So you're an old coot.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: I have a citation here in this folder from Rear Admiral Sprague.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What's this about, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: What's it say?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. It says, "In the name of the President of the United States, the Commander Carrier Division Three, Pacific, takes pleasure in presenting the Gold Star in lieu of Third Air Medal to Lieutenant (Junior Grade) Benjamin Evan Colkitt, Junior, United States Naval Reserve, for service as set forth as follows." And I can read that to you. Do you remember this?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What's this for?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Does it talk about the attack on the fleet in Kure?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yes. What about the attack?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: That was a good story. That was part of our preparations for the invasion. What was left of the Japanese fleet was tied up in Kure Harbor in the Inland Sea. So one of our jobs was to -- are we back on the record?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Okay. Good. So one of our jobs was to eliminate what was left of the Japanese fleet. So all planes from all the carriers. Was two days of strikes, and we eliminated what was left of the Jap fleet. And my target was carrier. And I was flying wing on the skipper, and both of us dropped on the carrier.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What was dropped on the carrier?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Both of us dropped our bombs on the carrier. And then after we dropped our bombs, we went through the old military maneuver of "Get the hell out of there." So we headed out to a rendezvous to go back to the ship. And the skipper started -- went down right off the water, flying down the Inland Sea. So here was the two of us flying down low to the water and into the sea in Indian country. And I'm sitting there, you know, "What in the hell are you doing? You're going to get us shot." It turns out what he was doing was locating pilots that had been shot down that were in the water, because at the beginning of the attacks, they would station rescue submarines on the edge of the area that's going to be attacked. And if you could make it to the submarine or the submarine could make it to you, they'd pick you up. And there's some real stories of courage, these submarine people that would come in and pick up the pilots. So we found out the skipper was just locating the pilots. There was something like 40 of them in the water after the attack. The guys had been shot down and gotten out. Never got shot.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Amazing.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: And I found out later -- in fact, I just found out a year ago -- that the Japanese launched one of their biggest attacks to counter our attack. They were saving their planes for the big attack, and they sent a bunch of them out after us during the attack, and I never saw a one. Never saw a one.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: You missed out, huh? I'm going to read a part of this, okay?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: It says, "He dove" -- speaking of you. "He dove low to drop his bomb on a large enemy carrier, despite intense and accurate anti-aircraft fire of all calibers." They come whizzing by your head?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. What they're -- what he's saying there is, this idiot didn't have sense enough to get the hell out of there before it was too late. But they had to brush it up a little bit.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And then it says -- now, I -- you're not going to explain this one away, too, okay? It says, "On retirement from the target, he flew through hazardous weather conditions to make a safe landing on the parent carrier." What were the hazardous weather conditions?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Storms. See, in those days, we didn't have the electronic navigation that you have now.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Right. So how did you find the carrier?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: It was -- by DR.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: The plotting board. So essentially just plot a wind vector. We estimated the wind, and had an estimate of where the carrier was, and this is strictly DR plotting.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Estimates. You have an estimate of where the carrier was.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, yeah. So it got -- it could get real exciting. That's what the young folks don't understand. Now they have all the goodies, the GPS and all that stuff. This was just the basics.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Amazing.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I remember one time, we flew back and a fog came in. So I had to get down to -- I don't have this one written down anywhere -- but we came back looking for the fleet, and we got down about 200 feet above the water, 'cause the fog was, oh, about 300 feet or so. And we came across the ship's wake. So I said, Well, wherever there's a wake, there's a ship. And so we flew down the wake till we found the ship, and then, well, if there's one ship, there's got to be others. So then we flew around till we found the carrier. And we didn't care whose carrier it was.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: I was going to ask if you knew it was yours.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. Any old carrier. So we flew around and we found the carrier and made an approach to it and landed on it. And what they did, if they got full of planes, they would push them over the side and make room for the others.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Bless their old hearts.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Wow. I had a question, and that totally blew my mind.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: A carrier is a carrier. So we were going to land there, and they knew it, so . . .

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And so it wasn't your carrier?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No. As a matter of fact, it wasn't.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Doesn't matter.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Couldn't have cared less.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And how many planes did they push over the side?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I have no idea.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: But it was war.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Did you have radio contact?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: We had radio, yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Was it clear? I mean, I know now, I'm sure it wasn't.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: It was basic.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Amazing.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, the electronics nowadays is amazing.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: It is.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: But that's what they're talking about there.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Well, I'm going to add one more thing. It says, "On 13 August 1945, he" -- you -- "participated in a successful attack on Matsushima" -- M-a-t-s-u-s-h-i-m-a --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: -- "Airfield Honshu" -- H-o-n-s-h-u --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah, Honshu is the main island.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. "-- where he took outstanding photographs of the action in spite of accurate and intense anti-aircraft fire of all calibers." Is that still the same, didn't get out of the way?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Very interesting.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: In what way?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: What they would do is, I'd go out to photograph the target, and they'd send four or five -- well, four or eight fighters along with me for protection, for escort. And this set up for a photographic run. They set up a flight line across the target, and the guys are back there supposed to be on the flanks for protection. And what would happen is, the Japs would shoot at me, and invariably, initially, they would not put enough lead in, so a lot of the shots were exploding behind me. Well, I could -- I would look in the mirror, and I could see them walking the shots up to me. So I'd add a little power, and then they'd fall behind, and then they'd start walking up again. By that time, I'd be through and get the hell out of there. Well, what happened was, the guys were supposed to stay on the beam, so when I added power, they fell behind, so they were back there where all the shots were going off, so they didn't care for this escorting duty. They didn't like it at all.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Well, I guess not.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, I said, "Come on, guys, keep up."

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And the last sentence of this citation from Rear Admiral Sprague says, "His courage and skill in carrying out and in performing his photographic mission were in keeping with the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service." Nice.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, to paraphrase, it means, the idiot, in spite of his stupidity, managed to get the job done, and he found the ship on the way home.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: You don't give yourself enough credit, it doesn't sound like at all.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Hey, there were two grades.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Pass and fail, huh? Do you recall the day that you retired? How did that feel?Benjamin Colkitt, II:: Yeah, I do. I didn't want to go. I wasn't ready to retire, but it was obvious I'd gotten too old, too senior, and there was nothing but a line of desks ahead of me. C. Kay Uhles:: And where was this that you finished your career?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And where is North Island again?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: San Diego.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: San Diego?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. You know, you know the time has come and it's time to go.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And what did you do right after you retired, just in the couple days or weeks?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Went to work with United.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: That soon? You didn't take any time off --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Nope.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: -- to go see the world?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Nope. I'd seen the world.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: You'd already seen the world.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. What had happened when I started setting up a retirement, I flew back to the Pentagon, and the commander at the desk said, "We can't possibly let you go, we don't have a replacement for you." So I went over to see a guy behind another desk, and he said, "Oh, sure, we can let you out any time you want." So I went back and I got two three-day leaves. So I was assuming the one that I wanted would pay off, so I drove on out here to Denver, to United, and took the job and went to work, 'cause at that time, the airlines were expanding like crazy.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What year was this, Ben?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: '64. So I came out to seem them, and they said, "Sure, you're hired. We want you to start working yesterday." So, well, I can handle that. So I started to work with two three-day leave papers in my pocket, and I was still in the Navy, and the retirement came through, and it was legal. So I really stepped out of the Navy into United.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And then how long did you serve for United?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: A little over 27 years.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And when did you retire from them, what year?

sp.speaker: Candace James
sp.p: Seems like you never truly retired. They would call you back in.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: '90 or '92, somewhere along in there.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: But you were still training people. They kept calling you after you retired.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: After I retired from United, they called me back on a contract basis to train some people.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: A Simulator?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. Worked out great for both of us.

sp.speaker: Candace James
sp.p: People were requesting you. It wasn't that -- you know, he had certain groups of people that really liked his training and specifically wanted him. Quite a few South American crews, right, that you had?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. See. (Ms. Colkitt enters room.)

sp.speaker: Donna Colkitt
sp.p: I don't want to miss out on the fun.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: They don't believe I picked you up at the bar.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Great stories. Did your military experience -- how did it affect the rest of your life? I mean, besides the obvious, I guess.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, that's pretty hard to answer. I don't think it did, really. I was lucky enough to be able to do what I wanted.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Does it -- how does it affect your thinking now about Iraq and Afghanistan?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, s-o-s.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Meaning?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Same old shit. The tragedy is, you know, you see it coming. But it's -- that's why I think this is so important. It's the same damn thing: Korea, Vietnam, the first flap over in Kuwait, and now Iraq. The same damn thing over again.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: So what should we do differently?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, we're not on the record?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: We are.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, in that case, stay the course.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: That's where you want to leave it?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, to me and my professional military compatriots, the way to run a business is to give an organization a job and let them do it. So what the government needs to do is decide what they want from the military, tell them what they want done, turn the military loose, and let them do it. Let them do their job.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Do you think they're doing it now?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Why don't you cut it.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Off the record?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. Okay. (Break.)

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. We can leave that. We can let that one go, then. Any -- you joined some organizations. Do you belong to the Tailhooks, did I hear?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What's that about?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, it's a group of pilots that get together occasionally and socialize and talk over engineering problems and professional problems.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Do you still meet with them?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: I can't get out.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: And Tailhook is an organization of retired and/or military pilots.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. Do you stay in contact with them now, even though you can't meet with them?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. The guys come by.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Do they?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Sounds like a special bond.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: It is. It is.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yeah. Did you attend reunions of your units or your --

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yeah? Any particular thing of humor, of interest, that you can tell us about?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: We had a reunion of Fighter Squadron 1 that flew in during the war. It was amazing. There were, I guess, something like 60 percent of the people showed up. But one ofthe amazing things was, though, there's something like 60 pilots in my squadron during the war, and three of us stayed in the military and continued flying and the rest went back to civilian. I couldn't understand that.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Wow. Yeah, that's not -- that's very small.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. But I got a story I need to tell you on the atomic bomb.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: In August of -- somewhere around the middle of the month, sitting in my Hellcat, fully fueled, fully armed, getting ready for a fighter sweep on a target in central Honshu, Japan.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: What year was this, Ben?

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: That was the middle of August, '45. And the word came down from primary flight to shut down our engines, 'cause we were turning up. We were ready to go. You know, what the hell is going on? So just shut down and return to the radio, which we did. And went downthere, and they said, "Operations for the day are canceled." You know, what the hell is going on? Nobody knew. Well, that's the way it is. Well, we found out later that's when they droppedthe first bomb, and our targets were close to their targets. And they didn't want Navy airplanes flying around there, so they took us out of the air for that strike. And then the -- a week or so later, the second bomb went off. Now, we didn't know it then, but we were preparing for the invasion of Japan, and we didn't know it then, but there's a good paper that I have somewhere that talks about the buildup that Japanese had on Kyoshu, which was going to be the first landing. And it was going to be one bloody affair. And so by dropping that bomb and stopping the war, it saved millions of lives. And we have these idiots that want to make the U.S. a villainfor dropping the bomb on those poor Japanese who started the war in the first place.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: American prisoners?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: No, Japs.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Japanese prisoners, okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Saipan. Even the civilians jumped off the cliff there. It was part of the Japanese attitude on life, not to be captured.

sp.speaker: Candace James
sp.p: So you're saying there was a lot of suicide? Is that what you were saying?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Oh, yeah. You know, on Saipan, on the south shore, big cliffs. And after we took the island, the civilians went down and jumped off that cliff, the women and children, rather than be captured. It was a vicious war. And the kids need to learn this. They need to learn the facts.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: You had mentioned Iwo Jima and that suicide, if I understood correctly. Was this before or after the bomb?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: The whole war.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: The whole thing.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: The whole war.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: It was part of their military society. So there's desperate, desperate need for the current generation to learn the history, 'cause somebody said, if you don't learn from history, you're doomed to repeat it.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Okay. And so your wife just showed me an e-mail that's talking about only a few Americans in 1945 were aware of an elaborate plan that had been prepared for the allied invasion of Japanese allies.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, we didn't know, and we didn't want to know.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: And that's when you were called off?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: When the bomb hit?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yeah. They were preparing us.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: And the first strike was -- was going to be on Kyoshu, and when they -- when the planners found out how many forces they were putting in there, they knew it was going to be a bloody one.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Is there anything, Ben, that you want to add that -- we're just about out of time. Is there anything that you want to add, any other stories or thoughts?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Can't think of it. I encourage the younger generation to look at the military as a profession. We need good people there. We also -- we need good people in the government. Patriotism. There's a crying need for it. And that's why this work is so important.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Well, I am sure grateful for you and your family to open your doors and let us come in and get your story.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, you want to see stories, we got sea stories.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Lots of stories. And I want to give you this certificate, Ben. This is a certificate just to thank you for your service, for the difference you've made in this country and this world. In my life, I know. Thank you. Thank you for your time.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Yep. My pleasure.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: All right. I think we're done.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Spread the word.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: We are. We are. We're going to get as many stories as we can.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: One of the biggest thrills I had during the war, after the surrender -- after the surrender, the fleet came into Tokyo Bay, and the surrender was signed on the Missouri. And so somebody came up with the idea, we got to have an air parade.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: An air parade?

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: An air parade. So when they were signing the surrender on the decks of the Missouri, all the planes from all the carriers, and even some Air Force, they rendezvoused and flew a parade over the signing. If you've ever seen any of the news reels on this, the sky was just black with airplanes. And I still remember, sitting in the cockpit, terrified, 'cause every place I looked, there's a piece of aircraft. There was no place to dodge. And you know, if my engine quits, this is going to get interesting, 'cause there were a thousand airplanes, quite a parade. And we got through it without hitting anybody. How I ever did that, I'll never know.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: That's interesting that that -- that scared you, where being shot at was part of the duty.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, when you look around, all you can see are propellers, it gets your attention.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Amazing. Amazing.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: So that was -- that was a big thrill.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: Amazing. I have seen news reels like that.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Well, you look in the middle of it and the Hellcat, and there I am.

sp.speaker: C. Kay Uhles
sp.p: There you are. Again, I thank you, Ben. This was awesome.

sp.speaker: Benjamin Colkitt, II
sp.p: Any time.
